atoms.text:
When Ethan, a 17‑year‑old student, came home from school, the living room was already occupied. His grandfather Karl, a retired engineer, sat in his favourite armchair reading a newspaper, while his mother, Nina, a 42‑year‑old, typed emails on her laptop at the kitchen table.

“Grandpa, you won’t believe what my teacher said today,” Ethan began, dropping his backpack with a thud. “He said my generation is too sensitive and spends more time on mental health than on maths.”

Karl snorted. “Well, he is not wrong, is he? In my day, we didn’t have time to talk about our feelings all the time. We worked hard, we respected authority, and we didn’t expect the world to adapt to us.”

atoms.a: What generations do Ethan, Karl and Nina (in this order) belong to?

wrong.text: Ethan is a Gen Z student, Karl is a Baby Boomer grandfather, and Nina is a Millennial employee.

atoms.text:
“That is such a Boomer thing to say,” Ethan replied, rolling his eyes. “You think hard work is the only answer to everything. You had cheap costs of living, stable jobs, and affordable housing. You have no idea what it’s like now.”

Nina looked up from her laptop. “Ethan, don’t dismiss your grandfather like that. But, Dad, you also have to admit things have changed. When I finished university, we hit the financial crisis, and now everything is more expensive. It’s not just ‘work hard and you’ll be fine’ anymore.”

Karl folded his newspaper. “Maybe. But at least your generation had some patience. You didn’t try to change the whole system overnight like these kids. All this talk about climate justice and quitting a job if it doesn’t feel meaningful—it sounds like entitlement to me.”

atoms.a: What are Ethan (Gen Z) and Karl (Baby Boomer) accusing each other of?
b: ++Ethan accuses Karl of living and especially thinking in the past.
Ethan accuses Karl of wanting to change the whole system in no time.
++Karl accuses Ethan of wanting special treatment.
Karl accuses Ethan of not having enough savings.

atoms.text:
Ethan crossed his arms. “It’s not entitlement, it’s survival. My generation is cleaning up all the mess left by yours. Climate change, student debt, mental health crisis. We’re just honest about it. And you call that ‘too sensitive’.”

Nina sighed. “Ethan, you also have to admit your teacher has a point sometimes. You are always on your phone. When I was your age, we didn’t have constant notifications. We had to wait for things. Maybe that did make us a bit more patient.”

“Wow, okay, here comes the Millennial lecture about ‘we knew the world before smartphones’,” Ethan shot back. “You all act like you’re the last ‘real’ generation, but you also spend hours scrolling and complaining about being burnt out. At least we talk openly about it.”

atoms.a: What are Ethan (Gen Z) and Nina (Millennial) accusing each other of?
b: ++Ethan accuses Nina of feeling superior to him based on her generation.
Ethan accuses Nina of being mentally unstable.
++Nina accuses Ethan of always being on the phone.
Nina accuses Ethan of being too patient.

atoms.a: What are the main issues for Ethan so far?
b: ++Neither his mom nor his grandfather seem to be able to fully understand his viewpoint.
++Nina and Karl both find reasons to degrade Ethan's viewpoint.
Nina and Karl don't allow him enough freedom to go out with friends.
Nina and Karl are jealous of his technological knowledge.

atoms.text:
In the next lesson, Ethan decided to stay behind after class.
“Mr. Winter, I want to say something about what you said yesterday. When you say my generation is too sensitive,” Ethan said, “it feels like you’re saying caring about our mental health is weak. We grew up with social media, crises, and constant bad news. Of course, we’re anxious. But that doesn’t mean we don’t work hard.”

Mr. Winter leaned against the desk. “I see your point. From my Gen X perspective, we were expected to just ‘deal with it’ alone. Maybe I mistake your openness for weakness and vulnerability because I was taught to stay silent.”

“And from my Gen Z perspective,” Ethan replied, “it feels like older generations think we’re lazy or addicted to our phones. Yes, we use technology all the time, but we also organise protests, share information, and learn new skills online. It’s not just wasting time.”

He nodded slowly. “I suppose every generation has its stereotypes. Maybe we all sometimes hide behind labels to avoid listening.”

Ethan said: “Exactly. I want you to see that we are so much more than just stereotypes. We just do things differently.”

atoms.a: What do Mr. Winter and Ethan agree on?
b: ++Because of stereotypes, other qualities in people are easily overlooked.
Mental health isn't an important topic.
Ethan's generation is lazy because of technology.
